title: Four Resorts, Four Seasons
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: The imaginary country of Calderia depends on visitors for a large part of its income, and the national tourist board has counted the number of guests at four well-known resorts in each season of last year. The figures show that the seasons matter a great deal: a resort that is crowded in July may be almost empty in January, and the reverse can also be true. Managers must therefore plan carefully, hiring staff only when they are needed and finding other work for the quiet months. This passage describes the pattern at each resort, using the board's charts, and considers what the managers do to survive.

The first resort is on the Golden Coast, a long stretch of sand and warm sea. It is busy in summer and autumn, when the water is warm enough for swimming, and the hotels are full from June to November. In winter and spring, however, the weather is cool and the sea is cold, and the number of guests falls to a small fraction of the peak. Most of the cafés and shops close for four months, and many workers return to their families inland or look for work in the fruit harvest. The hotel owners have long wished that they could attract visitors in the quiet months.

The second resort, in the Zandra mountains, has exactly the opposite problem. It is crowded in winter, when snow covers the slopes, and almost empty for the other three seasons. The skiers come from the cities, and they fill the hotels from December to March, paying high prices. In spring, summer and autumn, the lifts stand still and the shops are shut. The manager, Mr Dario Costa, has tried to change this by building a network of walking paths and a mountain bike park, but so far they have attracted only a small number of visitors in summer, and he says that it will take years before they make a real difference.

The third resort is the old city of Marin, famous for its palaces, museums and gardens. Its visitors come mainly in spring and summer, when the days are long and the streets are pleasant for walking, and numbers drop sharply in autumn and winter, when the weather is wet. The city has tried to spread the visitors over the year by holding festivals in the quiet months, and these have had some success. A winter music festival, now in its fifth year, fills many of the hotels in December, although the total is still lower than in the summer months.

The fourth resort is a spa town called Hallen, whose hot springs are said to cure many illnesses. Its pattern is unusual: it is busiest in spring and in winter, and it is quiet in summer and autumn. Doctors recommend that patients visit the spa in cool weather, when hot baths are most enjoyable, and in summer the heat makes the treatments uncomfortable. Many of the visitors are elderly and stay for two or three weeks. The owners say that this long stay is valuable to them, because a guest who stays for three weeks spends far more than a tourist who comes for a weekend.

Dr Beatriz Almeida, a tourism economist, studied all four resorts. She found that the resorts with only one busy season are the most at risk. When a wet summer ruins a beach season or a mild winter leaves the ski slopes bare, a year's income can be lost in a few weeks. She advises resorts to develop attractions that do not depend on the weather, such as conference centres, museums and covered swimming pools, so that visitors have a reason to come in every season. She also suggests that the board offer cheap tickets in the quiet months to encourage people to travel then.

The tourist board has accepted her advice and will begin a campaign next year. It will publish a calendar showing the events at each resort, and offer discounts for those who visit outside the peak. The board has also promised money to help resorts build new facilities, which will be repaid from the extra income. Critics say that the plan does not take account of the climate: a beach cannot be warm in January, whatever the board does. Supporters agree, but they reply that the aim is not to make every month equally busy, only to make the quiet months a little less quiet.
